newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to cut trade deficit at expense of growth.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to cut trade deficit at expense of growth.

text.p: South Korea's ecomony is expected to slow further next year as policymakers try to cut the country's snowballing current account deficit, officials and economists said on Friday.
"Defending our international payments status will take top priority in our economic policy next year," said Kim Young-dae, assistant governor of the Bank of Korea, the central bank.
"We certainly expect lower economic growth in 1997."
The central bank said on Friday it expected gross domestic product to grow a real 6.4 percent in 1997 against this year's estimated growth of 6.9 percent.
GDP, the value of a country's goods and services minus foreign income, grew 9.0 percent in 1995.
The economy had slowed largely due to a slowdown in exports and capital investment, bank officials said.
"We plan to put more emphasis on stability than growth next year. We may have to accept lower growth if we want to quickly improve the structural weakness of the economy," Kim said.
The central bank said on Thursday GDP grew a real 6.4 percent in the third quarter of this year, down from 9.8 percent in the year-earlier period.
The bank forecast the current account deficit would narrow to about $18 billion in 1997 from an estimated $22 billion this year.
"Our exports are likely to pick up in 1997 in line with the world's economic recovery," Kim said.
The bank said on Friday the current account deficit during the first 10 months of this year soared to $19.5 billion, more than double the $8.4 billion shortfall in the same period of 1995.
President Kim Young-sam this month ordered economic planners to draw up measures to cut the deficit drastically next year.
The South Korean economy ran into trouble early this year when plunging international prices began to dent the nation's major exports, especially semiconductors.

Memory chip producers, which accounted for nearly 20 percent of South Korea's total exports last year, were hit as prices for the 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips fell 70 to 80 percent from a year ago.
Semiconductor exports totalled $15 billion in the first 10 months of this year, down from $17.5 billion in the year-earlier period, according to government statistics.
"The fall looks small. But to earn that much we shipped four to five times the amount of chips we did last year," a trade ministry official said.

Industrial production remained robust to compensate for price falls. The National Statistical Office said on Friday industrial output rose 10.8 percent year-on-year in October, against a 9.9 percent rise a year ago.
Private sector economists said any measures to buoy the economy would only add to the ballooning deficit and fuel inflationary pressure.
"We may have to come to terms with lower growth because exports are unlikely to recover soon," said Kim Sung-shik, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
"The current account deficit now represents four to five percent of GDP. That is a dangerous level," he added.
The Bank of Korea said the deficit could fall to $13 billion next year if GDP growth were brought down to 5.5 percent.
